title: Nothing Is Shared Until You Synchronise: Reinterpreting Java for Data-Race Freedom
authors: Luke Cheeseman; Elias Castegren; David Black-Schaffer; Erik Österlund; Tobias Wrigstad
abstract: In mainstream shared-memory languages, programmers use synchronisation mechanisms such as locks to isolate shared data accesses across threads to avoid data races. Yet synchronisation enforces only a temporal ordering, while shared memory still communicates updates between threads at every ordinary read and write. To achieve isolation, programmers therefore need to understand the connection between ordering and communication, and to apply synchronisation correctly and consistently, while compilers and hardware optimise assuming they have. When programmers synchronise incorrectly, they lose isolation, and the semantics of their programs change without notice. We propose Sync-as-Share, a memory model built on isolation and communication rather than on the ordering of accesses to shared memory. We start from thread isolation, where each thread reads and writes a private view of memory, and reinterpret programs' existing synchronisation actions to also communicate updates explicitly. As nothing is communicated outside synchronisation actions, data races become impossible by construction. Instead, conflicting updates are detected at synchronisation points. Viewing synchronisation as explicit communication exposes the design decisions of what should be communicated, to whom, and what counts as a conflict. We propose two communication topologies with different trade-offs. We instantiate Sync-as-Share for Java by making the synchronisation actions already defined by its memory model the only points at which threads communicate, so Java programs can adopt Sync-as-Share unmodified. We formalise this instantiation as version-controlled memory, in which synchronisation actions push and pull updates between private views, and mechanise it in Rocq. We show that Java programs that are correctly synchronised under the Java memory model behave identically under shared memory and Sync-as-Share.

title: TOFS: Feature Selection with Swap Supervision for Semantic Communication over Fading Channels
authors: Zhiyi Zhu; Eiji Takimoto; Patrick Finnerty; Chikara Ohta
abstract: Task-oriented semantic communication transmits task-relevant features to support receiver inference under limited communication resources and adverse channel conditions. For image classification, the usefulness of a feature depends on the other transmitted features and the distortion introduced by the wireless channel. Effective feature prioritization should therefore account for classification performance after transmission of the selected features. This paper proposes a Task-Oriented Feature Selection (\textit{TOFS}) framework and method, which evaluates feature replacements using receiver classification loss. Loss differences confirmed under independent transmission samples provide pairwise ranking supervision for a selector network. The trained selector predicts priorities in a single forward pass. CIFAR-10 simulations demonstrate improved classification accuracy over an importance-based feature selection baseline at the same transmitted feature count and average transmit power. The proposed \textit{TOFS} framework shows 84\% accuracy performance under Rayleigh fading and Gaussian noise, compared with the 68\% performance of a SOTA method.

title: Semantic Extraction Framework for Goal-Oriented V2X Communication Supporting Safe Intersection Passage
authors: Haoran Yang; Shan Lu; Takaya Yamazato
abstract: This paper proposes a transmitter-side semantic extraction framework for goal-oriented Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) communication supporting safe intersection passage. Instead of transmitting raw sensory data, roadside infrastructure extracts task-relevant semantic information from video and traffic-signal sequences and organizes them into compact semantic packets for low-latency driving-decision assistance. The intersection-passing problem is formulated as a set of traffic tasks under Japanese traffic regulations, and the proposed pipeline generates perception and intent semantics through object detection, object tracking, region-of-interest (ROI)-based semantic extraction, and recommended-action generation. The framework is implemented and evaluated on a self-constructed, CARLA-based single-vehicle dataset collected under clear weather conditions. Experimental results show high recommended-action accuracy within the tested task set, while the mean processing latency remains below the frame interval of the 15~fps input video.

title: The Invisible Gap: Romanized Indic Generation Fails Where Automatic Metrics Succeed
authors: Madhu Sudhan Rao Beesetty; Surbhi Sharma; Devesh Maheshwari; Lokesh Meesala
abstract: Hundreds of millions of Indians communicate with digital systems in romanized Latin characters -- typing "aap kaise hain" rather than native script -- yet romanized Indic generation is absent from NLP benchmarks and evaluation frameworks. We demonstrate that automatic metrics (BGE-M3, BERTScore) systematically misrepresent the quality of romanized Hindi, Telugu, and Kannada generation. We evaluate four LLMs (Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Gemini 2.5-flash, Qwen3.5-35B) on 142 OpenAssistant query-response pairs. On a 72-response diagnostic subset, native speakers rate GPT-5.5 1.43 points higher than Claude Opus 4.8 on a 12-point rubric, whereas their full-dataset BGE-M3 means differ by only 0.004. Two distinct model-specific failure modes emerge: Gemini produces script spillage (16.9% of Telugu responses leak native script), while Qwen collapses to English-only output (16.2% of Kannada responses). We introduce a failure-aware evaluation policy that assigns zero to empty outputs, script-corrupted responses, and instruction collapses -- revealing failures metrics alone cannot detect. Our results show that evaluating romanized Indic generation requires a coordinated bundle: semantic similarity, script compliance, failure coverage, and native-speaker acceptability.

title: Dynamic signatures of collective knowledge through navigation in a network with semantic structure
authors: Abby Bertics; Elizabeth R. Chrastil; Jean M. Carlson
abstract: What distinguishes how humans navigate an information network like Wikipedia from what the underlying graph structure and language statistics alone predict? To study human collective navigation, we analyze 70,770 human trajectories through Wikispeedia, an online game where players navigate between articles to reach a target. To compare groups of trajectories rather than individual ones, we merge all trajectories leaving or entering a given article into a Flow Tree. Flow Trees compress collections of trajectories into hierarchies of group splits. We build forward and reverse Flow Trees for 815 of the most commonly traversed articles, representing divergence and convergence, respectively. We compare humans against four random-walker null models, either unweighted or weighted by graph structure, word frequency, or semantic similarity to target. Human Flow Trees are deeper with longer trunks and later splits, indicating players stay together longer than random walkers, whose Flow Trees tend to fan out immediately. An article's degree predicts 51.3-70.9% of the variation in Flow Tree branching factor for random walkers, but only 24.1-36.2% for humans. Taking what graph structure fails to predict as a two-dimensional coordinate system, we define four article types (beacons, funnels, forks, and corridors), distinguished by how humans enter and exit them. These human-defined types are not explained by out-degree or title-word frequency are, and are not recovered by any random walker. A fifth null model, built from first-order human click preferences, partially reproduces human Flow Tree shape but differs significantly in how much of that shape degree explains. We consider collective knowledge to be the structure shared by players who never communicate, beyond what graph structure imposes. It comprises first-order click preferences and a significant component that extends across clicks.

title: SCALE: Real-Time Latent Communication for Cyber-Physical Agents
authors: Shanghao Shi; Jian Xiao; Ching-Hsiang Chan; Sanjoy Baruah; Sastry Kompella; Yevgeniy Vorobeychik; William Yeoh; Ning Zhang
abstract: Latent communication enables agents to collaborate efficiently by directly exchanging intermediate model representations rather than raw sensor data or text messages. Existing approaches, however, are primarily designed for LLM agents and do not consider the bandwidth constraints and heterogeneous task deadlines faced by cyber-physical agents. In this work, we propose SCALE, a real-time latent communication method tailored for cyber-physical agents. Motivated by the spatio-temporal continuity of the physical world, SCALE matches tokens across consecutive latent messages using similarity scores to identify reusable information and avoid redundant transmission. It then profiles the semantic gain and communication cost of transmitting different amounts of latent information. Based on these profiles, SCALE employs a real-time scheduler that jointly determines which pending messages to transmit and how many latent tokens to send, subject to available bandwidth and task deadlines. We evaluate SCALE across three cyber-physical benchmarks and a physical spider robot case study under diverse network conditions and heterogeneous task deadlines. Our results show that SCALE significantly improves both task performance and on-time delivery in bandwidth-constrained networks. Our code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SCALE-4E80/.

title: AI-Native Task-Oriented Semantic Communications over a Relay: Benefits and Vulnerabilities
authors: Yalin E. Sagduyu; Tugba Erpek; Aylin Yener
abstract: Semantic communication (SemCom) using a relay node is considered, where the relay assists in conveying task-relevant information from a source to a destination, with meaning defined by classification labels. A joint end-to-end design of the source encoder, relay transformation, and destination decoders is developed to optimize both semantic inference accuracy and perceptual reconstruction quality for image data. Relay-assisted schemes are shown to outperform direct transmission, with gains that become more pronounced in low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) regimes across different relaying strategies. Alongside these performance benefits, however, a key security vulnerability introduced by the relay is identified, and a Byzantine attack is formulated in which the relay injects structured, learned perturbations into its transmitted signal. The attack operates on intermediate communication representations subject to channel effects, with perturbations generated through a learned mapping applied at test time. It is shown to significantly degrade semantic inference accuracy at the destination. These results reveal a clear trade-off between SemCom gains and security risks in relay-assisted systems, motivating the need for secure relay designs that account for insider threats.

title: SEER: A Scalable Event-Driven Runtime for Parallel Execution of Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Environments
authors: Jiming Su; Feng Zhu; Yuhao Xiao; Miao Zhang
abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is increasingly used in systems where many entities interact in a shared environment. In these workloads, policy inference can be batched on GPUs, but the CPU-side environment path still updates entity states, resolves local interactions, and builds observations inside each $\mathrm{env.step}$. This path can dominate latency in interaction-intensive workloads after policy batching. Existing vectorized environment interfaces and general event-driven runtimes do not directly address the fine-grained cross-entity work inside one bounded MARL step while preserving the step-level semantics expected by learning systems. We present SEER (Scalable Event-Driven Environment Runtime), a runtime for MARL environment execution under an explicit event-locality contract. SEER models each environment step as a bounded stream of timestamped events. If direct state updates are entity-local and cross-entity effects are represented as ordered future events, SEER can run independent events in parallel while preserving serial-equivalent boundary outputs. To make this contract practical, SEER uses a CAS-based dual-layer event queue: local event queues preserve per-entity causal order, while a parallel executive list exposes ready work to global worker threads. SEER further uses STPA, a preflight-guided thread-pool selection mechanism that combines short runtime traces with static workload and hardware features. We evaluate SEER on two parameterized MARL workloads: compute-intensive UAV swarm control (Aircraft) and communication-intensive wireless management (PCS). On Aircraft, SEER reduces inference latency by 16.2\% over the baseline. On PCS, SEER reduces environment-execution latency by 46.9\%, 19.5\%, and 64.9\% over ROSS-T, NBSE, and ROOT-Sim, respectively.

title: Technohybridism: Recursive Semantic Normalization in AI-Mediated Societies
authors: Charalampos M. Liapis; Epameinondas Panagopoulos
abstract: Language-generating AI systems are no longer only objects of linguistic interaction: their outputs increasingly re-enter the communicative and institutional practices from which their training material was drawn. Drawing on social theory, social epistemology, and the philosophy of language, this article develops a sociotechnical account of that re-entry. We introduce recursive semantic normalization: the process through which machine-generated formulations, once recurrently taken up, evaluated, reused, and institutionally retained, participate in the reproduction and transformation of semantic regularities. Under the heading of technohybridism, we argue that the relevant unit of analysis is the hybrid semantic system, a recursively coupled configuration of human practices, computational generation, and institutional uptake. First, we distinguish the concept from neighbouring accounts, including model collapse, looping effects, machine habitus, machine culture, and the epistemology of AI testimony. Second, we develop an analytical model that separates generation, selection, uptake, and persistence and distinguishes machine-attributable change from change that would have occurred anyway. Third, we analyse uptake as routinized, institutionally diffused, and socially stratified practice and state conditions under which machine-derived regularities become norms. Fourth, we identify social-epistemic consequences: the laundering of provenance that weakens epistemic vigilance, the erosion of the cognitive diversity on which collective inquiry depends, and the narrowing of shared hermeneutical resources. An evidential ladder for empirical research follows. The account attributes no normative authority to machine outputs; what changes is the field within which human and institutional uptake operates.

title: Operational Indirect Rate-Distortion Functions for Classification Tasks
authors: Yann Miguet; Elsa Dupraz; Philippe Mary
abstract: In goal-oriented communications, indirect source coding involves two sources: a semantic source $X$ and an observation $Z$, which is the only source available at the encoder. In this paper, we consider this framework for classification, where the decoder only needs to reconstruct $X$. We argue that the gap between the indirect rate-distortion function and the performance of practical learned coding schemes, such as variational information bottleneck (VIB) and variational autoencoder (VAE) architectures, comes from three effects: the latent representation, the choice of the deep neural network (DNN) architecture and training loss, and whether the encoder is aware of the task. To quantify these effects, we introduce four operational rate-distortion functions that account for the DNN architecture and the training loss, and we establish a hierarchy among them. We then derive these functions for a Gaussian mixture source, where $X$ is the mixture state. Numerical results, both for the Gaussian mixture and for practical coding schemes on the CIFAR-100 dataset, quantify the rate loss incurred by each effect.

title: DYNAMICS OF PORTFOLIO ASSESSMENT STRATEGY IN EVALUATING THE ENGLISH LANGUAGE SKILLS FOR PUPILS WITH HEARING IMPAIRMENTS IN FAKO DIVISION, SOUTH WEST REGION OF CAMEROON
authors: Ngenwie Emilia Tanyie; Therese Mungah Shalo Tchombe
venue: International Journal of Developmental Issues in Education and Humanities
abstract: This study examined the impact of portfolio assessment on evaluating the English language skills of pupils with hearing impairment in Fako Division, Cameroon. Portfolio assessment, as an informal and learner-centred approach, was explored within the framework of inclusive education, where traditional assessment methods often fail to adequately reflect the abilities of learners with hearing loss. The research utilised a quasi-experimental design involving pupils with hearing impairment in selected inclusive primary schools. Data were gathered through English language tests, classroom observations, and interviews with parents, teachers, head teachers, and the divisional delegate. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistics, t-tests, and regression analysis, while qualitative data underwent thematic analysis. The results indicated that pupils subjected to portfolio assessment performed significantly better in English language skills than those assessed through conventional methods. Statistical analysis (SPSS t-tests and regression) showed that pupils assessed via portfolios scored notably higher on post-tests (portfolio group mean=12.78 versus control=11.14; t(38)=2.919, p<.05). Regression analysis demonstrated that portfolio use was a strong predictor of language improvement (β=0.336, p<.001). Classroom observations and interview findings further revealed that portfolio assessment encouraged ongoing learning, increased learner engagement, self-reflection, and heightened teacher awareness of individual progress. The study concludes that portfolio assessment is an effective method for evaluating the English language skills of pupils with hearing impairment and recommends its systematic adoption within inclusive classroom practice.

title: From Embedded Finance to Embedded Obligation: A Law-and-Economics Theory of Consumer Protection in Platform-Mediated Financial Services
authors: Yongxin Chen
abstract: Embedded finance is usually described as the integration of financial services into non-financial platforms. This article argues that the deeper regulatory transformation is the embedding of future legal and economic obligations into ordinary consumption, work, business, and entertainment environments. When credit, payment, wage-advance, wallet, and merchant-financing functions are delivered through plat form architecture, consumer protection cannot focus only on the formal product or licensed provider. It must also examine how obligations are framed, made salient or obscure, personalized through data, and allocated across platforms, merchants, lenders, and technical intermediaries. The article develops a law and-economics theory of Embedded Obligation Architecture, explains its irreducible object, refines its four layers, and distinguishes it from choice architecture, digital nudging, dark patterns, behavioral contract theory, and platform governance. It specifies the evidentiary limits of transferring behavioral evidence to embedded-finance contexts and proposes a Functional Embedded Obligation Test as a standard with gateway elements, evidentiary thresholds, legal vehicles, safe harbors, and proportionate remedies.

title: The Sociolinguistics of Machine Identity: LLM Personality and Ideology Propagation
authors: Guangni Li
abstract: Do large language models (LLMs) possess a measurable "personality," and how do the linguistic properties of training corpora shape their cognitive style and downstream reasoning? This paper approaches these questions from a sociolinguistic perspective on machine "identity." This manuscript is positioned explicitly as a conceptual perspective paper: it does not present original experimental data, nor does it constitute a systematic review with defined search strategies or inclusion criteria. Instead, it synthesises key published findings into two original theoretical frameworks intended to guide future empirical and engineering work. We examine evidence that LLMs exhibit reliable, valid Big Five personality traits—particularly in large, instruction-tuned models—and that continued pre-training on domain-specific corpora may shape those traits through measurable linguistic features: imperative ratio, type-token ratio (TTR), and syntactic complexity. We then analyse how standard-language ideology embedded in training corpora is amplified in model outputs, disadvantaging dialect and minority-language communities. Building on these findings, we propose two conceptual contributions: (1) a Personality Engineering (PE) framework for targeted continued pre-training to cultivate task-appropriate cognitive profiles, and (2) a Language Ideology Propagation Model (LIPM) mapping the pipeline from corpus composition to societal impact. Both frameworks are explicitly conceptual and require empirical validation before they can function as operational guidelines. Their value lies in structuring future research and providing a shared vocabulary for cross-disciplinary collaboration, with direct implications for responsible AI deployment.

title: From Legal Databases to AI-Assisted Justice: A Risk-Sensitive Framework for the Application of Information Technologies in Law
authors: Li Yongxin
abstract: This paper analyzes information technologies in law and proposes a risk-sensitive framework for responsible digital legal practice. Using EU regulatory developments as the main legal lens, while also referring to international standards and policy materials, the study reviews legal databases, case-management systems, artificial intelligence and natural language processing, electronic identification and signatures, digital evidence, online dispute resolution and electronic courts. The paper's contribution is to connect general principles of transparency, human oversight, source verification and accountability to concrete stages of legal work: intake, research, drafting, identity assurance, signing, archiving and audit. Brief examples of AI-assisted drafting, online dispute resolution and electronic signature verification illustrate the practical use of the framework. The analysis concludes that digital legal systems create value when they remain traceable, proportionate and subject to professional responsibility rather than replacing legal judgment.

title: Measuring Activity-Space Segregation with Multi-Source Big Data: A Physical--Digital Framework with Simulation Validation and a Real-Data Proof of Concept
authors: Guangwei Wang
abstract: Segregation research increasingly measures who people encounter beyond home, yet physical mobility, place semantics, and digital activity are often combined without clear construct boundaries. This study develops a physical--digital activity-space framework that distinguishes co-presence, digital exposure, and digital interaction, and represents physical and digital segregation as separate components rather than a forced composite. Validation is deliberately split by evidentiary role. A public Washington--Baltimore Foursquare check-in subset tests the computational feasibility and robustness of a discrete group co-visitation statistic; it does not validate continuous socioeconomic exposure because the dataset lacks individual socioeconomic status. Monte Carlo experiments separately test layer-selective construct response and sensitivity to trace missingness, spatial aggregation, socioeconomic measurement error, and cross-layer coupling. The results show that the proposed calculations are executable and that the synthetic physical and digital components respond selectively to their generating mechanisms, while also revealing important measurement attenuation. No real-data estimate of income segregation, digital exposure, physical--digital coupling, or the causal effect of inequality is reported. The framework therefore combines bounded validation with a falsifiable comparative and causal research agenda.

title: From Chopin to Kitsch? Pauline Viardot's Vocal Mazurkas and the popularisation of classical music
authors: Stacy Olive Jarvis
venue: Journal of Music Theory and Transcultural Music Studies
abstract: This article examines the concept of ‘popular music’ in the context of the work of Frédéric Chopin (1810–1849). The paper analyses six mazurkas by the Polish composer and their transcription for voice and piano, performed by the opera diva Pauline Viardot (1821–1910) to words by the French poet Louis Pomme (1831–1901). This chamber vocal cycle, composed by Viardot, illustrates the established poetics of the salons of the second third of the 19th century, where literature and music converged. Based on an analysis of various sources, this study examines the history of the works’ creation, their imagery and intonation, as well as the harmonic features of these vocal miniatures, whilst reconstructing their context. As a result, a connection is revealed between Viardot’s vocal mazurkas and Chopin’s songs, composed between 1829 and 1847, in the themes of love and loneliness. The aim of this article is to investigate how the opera singer bridges the gap between classical music and the mass audience and becomes a creator of kitsch. The research methodology includes an analysis of historical sources, as well as a musical and literary analysis of Chopin’s and Viardot’s mazurkas. The author concludes that kitsch emerges at the intersection of classical and popular music, where the integration of various elements from different mazurkas helps Viardot achieve a precise correspondence between the expressive content of the text and Chopin’s musical language.

title: Video and digital games: Historical controversies, benefits, and risks for children and adolescents
authors: Hanna David
venue: Journal of Child Development, Exceptionality and Education
abstract: Video and digital games have been the focus of sustained public and scientific debate since their commercial emergence in the late 1970s, particularly regarding their effects on children and adolescents. Early public and scientific discourse frequently portrayed gaming as a source of physical injury, addiction, aggression, social isolation, academic problems, and moral decline. However, subsequent empirical research has produced a substantially more differentiated picture of both the benefits and risks of gaming. This review examines the historical foundations of controversies surrounding video and digital games and synthesizes contemporary evidence concerning their cognitive, emotional, social, therapeutic, and physical effects. . Research indicates that moderate, purposeful gaming may improve visuospatial abilities, attentional control, problem-solving, mood regulation, social connection, and selected educational outcomes. Gaming-based interventions have also demonstrated therapeutic potential, particularly for depressive symptoms and attention-related difficulties among young people. At the same time, important risks remain, especially when gaming becomes excessive, compulsive, or disruptive to everyday functioning. These include repetitive-strain injuries, sleep disruption, problematic gaming, and adverse mental-health and academic outcomes. Evidence concerning violent games and serious real-world aggression remains more contested, with recent research emphasizing relatively small effects and the importance of individual and contextual factors. Overall, the evidence suggests that the developmental consequences of gaming for children and adolescents depend less on gaming itself than on the duration, content, context, and pattern of engagement.

title: Triage models for surgical decision-making in patients with shoulder pain: an integrative review.
authors: Samah Hassan; Kenneth J Faber; Joy Christine MacDermid
abstract: Shoulder pain is a major cause of work absenteeism, affecting 1 in 3 adults. Although nonsurgical treatments like physical therapy are recommended as the first line of management, 40% of patients are referred for surgery before exploring these options. This review aimed to identify existing triage models used for shoulder pain referrals for surgery, guidelines for shoulder pain management that include criteria for surgical referral, and indications for surgery. An integrative review approach was used to comprehensively search major databases (Medline, PubMed, Embase, CINAHL Plus) and gray literature. Articles on triage models, referral processes, or surgery candidacy for shoulder pain were included. The searches retrieved 4510 articles, with 480 selected for full review and 71 articles included in this synthesis. Thirty-seven articles described various triage models and clinical decision-making processes for managing shoulder pain, including determining when to refer for surgical consultation and the indications for surgery. Seventeen articles compared surgical and nonsurgical treatments to identify surgical indicators, 10 articles examined factors affecting decision-making, and 7 articles explored predictor models for surgical outcomes. The findings underscore the need for a multifactorial decision-making process that acknowledges the complexity of pain within a biopsychosocial framework and incorporates patients' personal preferences into the triage decision-making process. These triage models should work across different contexts, eg, conservative, primary, and speciality care, to facilitate better patient experience across the continuum.

title: The RAIL Principles for Neurosymbolic AI: Reasoning, Assurances, Interfacing and Learning
authors: A. d'Avila Garcez
abstract: Neurosymbolic AI systems that integrate machine learning and symbolic reasoning are rapidly gaining attention. They complement the data-intensive statistical approaches of neural networks and language models with symbolic reasoning formalism and algorithms to function in high-stakes domains or in low-data regimes that characterize many real-world applications. We argue that the neurosymbolic combination of machine learning and formal reasoning is not a niche approach within AI, but rather includes many already successful techniques that are of crucial importance to the development of reliable, efficient and, ultimately, trustworthy systems. This perspective prompts a re-examination of the design of current AI systems. We show that many leading AI systems can be analysed from the perspective of four principles of neurosymbolic AI design: Reasoning, Assurances, Interfacing and Learning (RAIL). Applying the RAIL framework offers a unified view of seemingly disparate AI systems, ranging from physics-aware machine learning to DeepMind’s Alpha-* suite, causal learning and tool-augmented Large Language Models. Importantly, using the neurosymbolic RAIL principles as a much-needed new evaluation standard for AI will enable engineers to make better-informed and more principled decisions about the design and deployment of production-level AI systems. In this article, we introduce the RAIL principles, examine how they can be applied across major areas of AI, and illustrate how they may guide practitioners to integrate neurosymbolic methods into next-generation AI technologies.

title: From Prompt to Pwn: Exploiting GPU Memory Errors During ML Inference
authors: Jonas Roels; Adriaan Jacobs; Silviu Vlasceanu; Mahmoud Ammar; Stijn Volckaert
abstract: GPUs accelerate a growing fraction of modern computing workloads.While prior work has studied the exploitation of memory errors in GPU applications written in C/C++ dialects, existing attacks rely on artificially introduced memory errors that grant attackers capabilities that may not arise when exploiting real-world GPU software.Consequently, GPU vendors and developers continue to largely treat such errors as reliability concerns rather than security issues, leaving vulnerabilities unpatched and potentially exploitable.This paper challenges that assumption.We show, for the first time, that remote, unprivileged adversaries can trigger device-side memory errors in realistic ML applications under specific conditions.We develop controlled proof-of-concept exploits that escalate vulnerabilities in the PyTorch ML framework and the CuDF dataframe library into write-what-where primitives, and weaponize such errors to enable denial-of-service, targeted manipulation and degradation of ML models, sensitive data leakage, and device-side code injection.To facilitate exploit construction, we design and implement a dynamic taint-tracking framework for NVIDIA GPUs that tracks attacker-controlled data flows to identify exploitable memory objects.Our findings demonstrate that adversaries can conduct memory-corruption attacks on vulnerable ML inference servers, highlighting the need to reassess prevailing assumptions about GPU memory safety and adopt essential mitigations, such as Write-XOR-eXecute, that are currently absent from modern GPUs.

title: End-to-End Hardware Validation of OSSDM Semantic Waveform for 6G Communications
authors: Lahcen Attijani; Panagiotis Vlachos; Mohamed Amine Hamoura; Emilio Calvanese Strinati; François Rivet
abstract: Future networks are evolving toward semantic communications, where preserving task-relevant information becomes more important than ensuring bit-level reliability. Recent work introduced Orthogonal Semantic Sequency Division Multiplexing (OSSDM), a Walsh-based semantic waveform that outperformed semantic OFDM (S-OFDM) in simulation. However, its end-to-end performance over a real wireless link remained unverified. This paper presents, to the best of the authors’ knowledge, the first hardware demonstration of an OSSDM-based semantic communication system using a Universal Software Radio Peripheral (USRP) X310 software-defined radio (SDR) at 2.45 GHz. CIFAR-100 images are transmitted through OSSDM and an S-OFDM baseline, and evaluated using classification accuracy as the task-level metric. While both systems achieve a similar Tx-side accuracy ceiling of about 76%, OSSDM consistently preserves higher accuracy after wireless transmission. These results provide the experimental validation that the robustness gains of OSSDM observed in simulation translate into improved task-level performance over a real wireless channel

title: Knowledge Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Schema Matching
authors: Chuangtao Ma; Sriom Chakrabarti; Arijit Khan; Bálint Molnár
venue: ACM Transactions on Knowledge Discovery from Data
abstract: Traditional similarity-based schema matching methods fail to resolve semantic ambiguities and conflicts in complex, domain-specific mappings due to a lack of commonsense and domain-specific knowledge. In parallel, large language models (LLMs) without sufficient background knowledge tend to hallucinate, further complicating schema matching. To overcome these limitations, we introduce KG-RAG4SM, a Knowledge Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Schema Matching. This method integrates novel retrieval mechanisms, including LLM-based, vector-based, graph traversal-based, and hybrid techniques with advanced reranking schemes to extract the most relevant subgraphs from large external KGs. Our approach achieves superior results without requiring re-training, as evidenced by improvements of 39.79% in precision and 30.56% in F1 score over LLM-based state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods (e.g., Jellyfish-8B) on the MIMIC dataset, and enhancements of 69.20% in precision and 21.99% in F1 score over pre-trained language model (PLM)-based SOTA methods (e.g., SMAT) on the Synthea dataset. Additionally, KG-RAG4SM scales effectively across KGs from commonsense KGs to domain-specific ones, while its instruction-tuning knowledge exclusion component ensures truthful performance in end-to-end schema matching tasks despite the suboptimal relevance of KG context. Our empirical analysis and case studies from real-world scenarios show that the hallucination problem in LLMs for schema matching is well mitigated by our solution.

title: Structured Agentic Learning for Persistent Spatial Acquisition in RDT-TAIS-Assisted Communications
authors: Bin Liu; Wei Ni; Tommy Svensson; Sofie Pollin
abstract: Persistent TAIS operation can reduce repeated radio-information acquisition by reusing environmental knowledge across control intervals. This knowledge changes with radio-environment evolution and current communication task. This paper studies persistent spatial knowledge maintenance for TAIS control and formulates it as a sequential information-acquisition problem that maximizes effective communication performance while accounting for physical-acquisition overhead under an outage-reliability constraint. We develop structured agentic spatial intelligence (ASI), which realizes a communication-oriented agent that maintains persistent spatial knowledge, forms beliefs from radio and context observations, and adapts physical information acquisition through closed-loop interaction with the radio environment. By jointly exploiting radio-consistent context inference, temporal knowledge-sufficiency assessment, graph-structured regional reasoning, and predictive outage-risk feedback, structured ASI determines when additional acquisition is needed, where it is directed, and how much physical information is sufficient before stopping or escalating to full radio-environment reacquisition. Numerical results show that structured ASI improves the effective rate by 2.59% while reducing acquisition overhead by 25.0% at six structural changes per 100 control intervals, and achieves a 2.82% effective-rate gain with a 41.8% overhead reduction over a heterogeneous 400-interval mission.

title: Integrated Identity Protection for Semantic Communications in Embodied IoT Systems
authors: Yu Zhang; JingQi Liu; Shuangrui Zhao; Yuanyu Zhang; Yulong Shen; Xiaohong Jiang
abstract: Embodied Internet of Things (IoT) systems are promoting the adoption of task-oriented semantic communication (SemCom), in which the trustworthy task decisions require both semantic information reliability and source legitimacy. However, existing trustworthy designs in SemCom mainly focus on semantic content recovery and protection, with limited attention to source legitimacy. Motivated by this limitation, this paper establishes a new information exploitation paradigm for integrated SemCom-identity protection to address active source impersonation and passive identity inference by treating each SemCom signal as an inherent carrier of both task-relevant semantic information and transmitter physical identity information. We first examine these two information resources and then analyze their integration feasibility at the observation, processing, and decision levels. To exploit these resources for trustworthy decision making, we further develop a dual-branch identity protection mechanism under different operating modes. In the authentication mode, semantic recovery and physical-layer source verification are performed in parallel using the same received observation. In the concealment mode, identity exposure is suppressed while semantic recovery quality is maintained to support anonymous sensing reports. The resulting outputs are jointly interpreted to support task decisions under mode-specific identity protection requirements. Finally, two representative case studies on active source impersonation and passive identity inference are presented to evaluate the proposed framework.

title: Building a Method: Challenges and Lessons from Developing an Impact Evaluation Framework for Public Investment in Open Source Software
authors: Laia Domenech Burin
abstract: Modern societies and institutions depend on an invisible layer of open digital infrastructure: foundational, openly accessible digital technologies that support a broad range of social and economic activities. Open source software is a core component of this infrastructure, underpinning everyday technologies and critical systems in various critical sectors. As open source software becomes increasingly recognised, funded, and governed as open digital infrastructure, policymakers face growing demands for accountability, transparency, and credible evidence of impact. However, methods for evaluating public investment in open source software remain underdeveloped, with no widely accepted methodological standard. This paper describes the Sovereign Tech Agency's transition from qualitative reporting and funding-recipient self-assessment towards a mixed-methods approach that incorporates quantitative, goal-oriented evaluation to inform funding decisions. Drawing on the development of this framework, it examines its initial design, the practical and structural challenges encountered, and the responses adopted. The work identifies three central challenges: evaluation indicators must reflect heterogeneous project goals and contexts; quantitative assessment relies on fragmented and fragile data infrastructure; and observed changes before, during, and after investment do not establish causal attribution without additional research designs. The paper argues that evaluating investment in open source software is not only a methodological task but also a governance practice, dependent on sustainable open research infrastructure, community knowledge, and ongoing methodological refinement.

title: Spectral-Convolutional Factorized Transformer for Joint Multipath Parameter Estimation: Applications to mmWave Positioning and Radio SLAM
authors: Yaya Etiabi; Wessam Ajib; Halima Elbiaze
abstract: Future 6G wireless networks are expected to evolve toward AI-native systems that support intelligent, environment-aware services, including positioning and mapping. Current research has already integrated AI into several aspects of communication, particularly wireless channel estimation. However, most learning-based channel estimators focus on communication-oriented objectives rather than explicitly estimating multipath parameters such as delay, angle of arrival (AoA), and angle of departure (AoD). These parameters provide essential geometric information for downstream tasks including positioning and radio simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM). In this work, we propose a Spectral-Convolutional Factorized Transformer (SCFT) for joint multipath component (MPC) estimation from noisy complex channel estimates and physical beam-pair descriptors. SCFT combines local spectral convolution, permutation-equivariant beam-set attention, and a query-based Transformer decoder to detect and classify line-of-sight (LoS) and non-line-of-sight (NLoS) paths and estimate their observed delays, AoAs, and AoDs. Experiments on realistic ray-tracing data show that SCFT reduces the generalized optimal sub-pattern assignment (GOSPA) error by 13.4% compared with ResNet, the strongest competing baseline. We further demonstrate this advantage in independent snapshot positioning and radio SLAM, where SCFT reduces position RMSE by 18.5% and 65.0%, respectively, relative to ResNet. These findings highlight the importance of explicitly recovering multipath geometry, as improvements in MPC estimation can translate into substantial gains in downstream tasks.

title: Synergy-Aware Symbol Allocation for Distributed Semantic Communication
authors: Fan Gao; Youzheng Wang; Zhijin Qin; Xiaoming Tao
abstract: Distributed semantic communication enables spatially separated terminals to support collaborative inference over wireless links for 6G edge intelligence. In multimodal sensing and cooperative perception, a single terminal captures only a partial view, and full task semantics emerge only when complementary observations from multiple terminals are fused at the receiver. However, under tight uplink budgets, existing task-oriented joint source--channel coding (JSCC) and distributed information bottleneck (IB) methods evaluate rate--distortion trade-offs per terminal, tending to undervalue cross-terminal synergistic features and prune them prematurely. To address this issue, we propose a synergy-credited distributed JSCC (\method{}) framework that introduces a differentiable, post-equalization matrix Rényi synergy credit as a surrogate to reward complementary task evidence surviving the wireless channel and backpropagates its gradients to local symbol gates. At deployment, the credit branch is removed and binary symbol masks are frozen, allowing each terminal to encode independently without inter-terminal signaling or extra inference overhead. Experiments show that \method{} recovers the analytical symbol-selection threshold on parity sources and reduces payload symbols by 28.4\% on AV-MNIST and 32.9\% on PAMAP2 over an uncredited gated baseline, while achieving a 6.2-point accuracy gain at $-6$~dB under 3GPP TDL-C fading with pilot-aided channel estimation for low-overhead wireless cooperative sensing.
keywords: task-oriented communication; semantic-aware communication; semantic channel coding

title: Embodied Movable Antennas
authors: Yewen Cao; Dengke Wei; Yulin Shao
abstract: This paper introduces embodied movable antennas (MAs), a new MA architecture that rethinks the source of antenna mobility. Unlike conventional MAs that rely on dedicated antenna actuators, embodied MAs harness the mechanical degrees of freedom already present in physical agents to reconfigure antenna position and orientation. We distinguish two modes of embodied MAs: task-coupled and task-preserving. Focusing on the latter, we show how wireless channels can be reconfigured by exploiting task-equivalent host configurations without altering the prescribed physical task. Using a redundant robotic manipulator as a canonical realization, we characterize the intrinsically coupled antenna translation and orientation induced by task-preserving self-motion and derive an exact Fourier representation of the resulting multipath channel. Our analysis reveals that the wireless value of embodied mobility depends not merely on how far an antenna can move, but on which configurations remain feasible under the physical task and how their coupled motion interacts with polarization and multipath propagation. Building on this insight, we develop a cross-task antenna mounting design that enables wireless adaptation with a fixed physical installation. Numerical results demonstrate substantial communication gains through task-preserving motion. These findings establish mechanical redundancy as a new, quantifiable resource for wireless channel reconfiguration.

title: The Role of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Korean Language Learning: Applications, Challenges, and Instructional Strategies
authors: Yundong Wu
abstract: This conceptual narrative review examines the role of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in Korean language learning. The paper synthesizes recent scholarship on AI-assisted language learning, Korean language education, technology acceptance, and educational ethics to develop an analytical framework for responsible classroom use. The review focuses on four dimensions: Korean language skills, Korean-specific linguistic and cultural features, instructional design, and governance risks. The analysis suggests that generative AI can support listening, speaking, reading, and writing when tasks are explicitly designed around Korean phonology, morphology, pragmatics, and learner purposes such as TOPIK preparation, study abroad, employment, and popular-culture engagement. It also identifies challenges in cultural-pragmatic accuracy, hallucinated expressions, assessment validity, data privacy, unequal access, teacher readiness, and learner dependency. The paper concludes that generative AI should function as a mediated learning resource rather than a substitute for teachers, learner judgment, or culturally grounded interaction.

title: Research on Attention Guidance and User Autonomy in AI-Powered Immersive Environments
authors: Mulin Qiao
abstract: As artificial intelligence gets deeply embedded into immersive environments, attention-guiding technology delivers ever more precise and efficient outcomes. Still, this improved efficiency carries an overlooked design risk: excessive AI guidance may steadily erode user agency and undermine exploratory behaviors as well as the process of meaning-making. This paper builds a critical conceptual framework to rethink attention-oriented design within AI-driven immersive settings. It defines excessive guidance and establishes theoretical links between this concept and three core facets of user agency: perceived control, voluntary choice and decision-making authority. Based on these findings, the paper calls for a paradigm shift from attention optimization to curiosity-led design. It also puts forward actionable behavioral measurement indicators covering exploration scope, average dwell time, path-following ratio, active choice frequency and recall test performance. The proposed framework supplies a new theoretical tool for human-computer interaction research in immersive scenarios and helps shift AI's role from a fixed route provider to an exploratory collaborator.

title: Antitrust Regulation of Algorithmic "Platform-Driven Involution'': From Governing the Corporate Person to Governing the Platform Ecosystem
authors: Sida Zeng
abstract: Digital platforms increasingly govern competition through algorithmically administered rules that allocate visibility, subsidies, commissions, participation opportunities, and sanctions. This article reconstructs ``platform-driven involution'' as a testable, portfolio-based theory-of-harm framework rather than a freestanding antitrust offense. Its application remains anchored in market definition, dominance, identified conduct under Article 22 of China's Anti-Monopoly Law, causal proof, competitive effects, and objective justification. The article clarifies that ecosystem analysis supplements rather than replaces relevant-market analysis and develops an evidence architecture for separating platform-induced effects from macroeconomic, demand, cost, and merchant-specific confounders. It then distinguishes preventive measures already supported by Chinese hard law or voluntary compliance guidance from compulsory competition-specific filing and pre-deployment assessment that would require clearer future authorization. The 2026 Trip.com decision is used to show how traffic allocation, exclusivity, lowest-price requirements, technical monitoring, and sanctions can form an integrated abuse architecture while liability remains tied to established statutory categories. Comparative analysis of EU platform regulation and Google Shopping supports calibrated procedural prevention, meaningful explanation, and causal discipline without protecting inefficient competitors or condemning aggressive competition.

title: Digital-Twin-Driven Predictive Maintenance and Fault-Tolerant Control for Electrified Agricultural Machinery: A Multiphysics and Deep Reinforcement Learning Framework for PMSM In-Wheel Drives
authors: Hongyu Xia
abstract: Electrified agricultural machinery increasingly relies on permanent-magnet synchronous motor drives that must remain dependable under variable traction, terrain-induced vibration, thermal cycling, contamination, and intermittent duty. Existing work offers mature methods for motor fault diagnosis, digital twins, predictive maintenance, and distributed-drive fault-tolerant control, but their health information is often not shared across diagnosis, maintenance, and control. This article develops a multiphysics digital-twin framework in which electrical, thermal, mechanical, and vibrational evidence maintains a probabilistic health belief that constrains both supervisory maintenance decisions and torque redistribution. The framework formalizes observability, uncertainty-aware health factors, deterministic safety shielding, multi-rate fallback logic, and agriculture-specific traction constraints. Reproducible low-fidelity numerical studies provide preliminary support for context-conditioned residual diagnosis and the revised thermal-continuity trade-off underlying health-aware derating, including robustness and sensitivity analyses. They do not validate sim-to-real transfer or the reinforcement-learning policy itself; those hypotheses remain open for dynamometer and hardware-in-the-loop testing. The results are therefore interpreted as mechanism-level evidence rather than field-performance validation.

title: Screen use in children and adolescents: Developmental risks, benefits, and educational implications
authors: Hanna David
venue: Journal of Child Development, Exceptionality and Education
abstract: The “war against screens” — the intense parental and societal pushback against children’s and adolescents’ excessive use of smartphones, social media, tablets, and games — was lost from the outset. Modern life is inseparable from screens; even closed communities fail at total prohibition. Cross-national parent movements (Wait Until 8th, Smartphone Free Childhood) and policy responses (age restrictions, phone-free schools in Australia, Brazil, Europe, etc.) reflect these worries. Practical guidance centers on the Surgeon General’s “5 Ds” (Discuss, Do, Delay, Divert, Disconnect) and family media plans rather than prohibition. Historical roots of techno-skepticism are traced to Weizenbaum (1976) and Dreyfus. Part 2 focuses on doomscrolling (“catastrophe scrolling”) – compulsive consumption of distressing news. Evolutionary negativity bias, amygdala activation, and dopamine loops sustain the behavior. Gifted adolescents are particularly vulnerable due to intellectual hyperarousal, high empathy, and still-maturing self-regulation. Preliminary group interventions using gradual behavior shaping show promise in reducing the habit. Part 3 dismantles the popular notions of “brain rot” (Oxford Word of the Year 2024) and Spitzer’s “digital dementia.” Neither is a clinical entity; rigorous evidence for permanent cognitive atrophy from screen use is lacking. Content and context matter far more than the medium itself. Paradoxically, technology use in older adults is associated with lower cognitive-decline risk. Both terms remain useful only as red flags for problematic, addictive patterns that impair sleep, mood, and functioning. Overall, screens cannot be eliminated, but intentional limits, high-quality content, protected sleep, real-world activities, parental modeling, and platform accountability can substantially mitigate risks. The goal is not victory in a lost war, but wiser coexistence.

title: STEM E-MODULE DEVELOPMENT WITH DEMONSTRATION MEDIA FOR LINEAR MOTION
authors: Risva Maharani; Afrizal Mayub; Silvia Syeptiani
venue: University of Bengkulu Scholar Repository (University of Bengkulu)
abstract: This study aims to develop a STEM-based E-Practicum Module assisted by a line-follower robot demonstration to support junior high school students’ understanding of the concept of object motion. The study used the Research and Development (R&D) method with the 4D model, limited to the Development stage. A limited pilot test involving 30 seventh-grade students used a one-group pretest-posttest design. The results showed that the E-Practicum Module achieved a validity percentage of 91%, categorized as “highly valid,” and a readability score of 93%, categorized as “highly acceptable.” Students’ conceptual understanding improved after the implementation of the e-module, as indicated by an N-Gain score of 0.8696, categorized as “high.” Based on the measured indicators, the “identifying” indicator achieved the highest N-Gain value, while the “analyzing” indicator achieved the lowest N-Gain value. The novelty of this study lies in the integration of STEM-based laboratory activities with a line-follower robot demonstration within a single e-module to connect the concept of motion with physical phenomena that can be directly observed and measured. This integration provides a contextual learning experience that supports students in observing, measuring, and interpreting the concept of motion. The results of the study indicate that the developed E-Module for laboratory activities can be used as teaching material in the study of object motion in junior high school.

title: On the Optimality of Implicit Feedback in Markov Decision Processes over Imperfect Links
authors: Romain Planchon; Federico Chiariotti; Federico Mason; Andrea Zanella; Deniz Gunduz
abstract: Goal-oriented communication protocols are explicitly designed to support the objectives of target applications, such as the monitoring and control of remote processes, while minimizing data traffic. This study considers a transmitter node that observes the environment state and sends it to a remote agent, which then performs control actions. This problem can be modeled as a remote Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP), a subclass of decentralized POMDPs. Existing studies limit transmissions through communication costs, but neglect the effect of channel impairments and non-ideal or delayed feedback. In this work, we study the optimal joint transmission and control policies over lossy forward channels without explicit acknowledgments. We introduce \emph{revealing} policies, under which the receiver's action, observed directly by the transmitter, discloses the outcome of the forward transmission, keeping the two agents synchronized without a feedback channel. We derive sufficient conditions for the optimality of time-invariant policies in this implicit feedback regime for general POMDPs, along with strictly weaker sufficient conditions in the special case of contextual bandits. Our simulations over a family of remote POMDPs show that these conditions are conservative, and revealing policies are optimal over a substantially wider parameter range than the conditions warrant.

title: AI-Aided and AI-Oriented Integrated Sensing, Communication, and Computation: A Survey
authors: Yaya Etiabi; Wessam Ajib; El Mehdi Amhoud; Halima Elbiaze
abstract: The evolution from 5G to 6G networks marks a transition toward the "intelligence of everything." While 5G enables enhanced connectivity, 6G aspires to embed intelligence directly into communication infrastructures, creating systems that are adaptive, context aware, and capable of autonomous decision making. Realizing such systems depends on harmonizing three fundamental functions that compete for shared network resources and often pursue conflicting goals: (i) sensing for environmental and contextual information acquisition, (ii) communication for reliable and timely information exchange, and (iii) computation for information processing and decision making. This harmonization necessitates shifting from independent optimization to their joint design as a unified system, a paradigm known as Integrated Sensing, Communication, and Computation (ISCC). In parallel, AI has emerged both as an enabling tool for ISCC optimization and as a workload whose requirements influence ISCC system design. This survey comprehensively examines ISCC from this dual perspective by distinguishing between AI-aided ISCC, in which learning-based methods support the joint design and optimization of sensing, communication, and computation, and AI-oriented ISCC, in which these functions are jointly configured to support learning, inference, and distributed intelligence. The survey further examines the co-design of AI and ISCC, where AI requirements and ISCC constraints jointly shape system and model decisions. It further provides a comparative synthesis of the resulting design approaches, system architectures, performance metrics, and evaluation practices, relates these developments to application-specific requirements across different domains, and identifies open research problems toward scalable, adaptive, and trustworthy AI-ISCC systems.

title: Crossing the Chasm: Bridging Visual Augmentations and Designer Intent
authors: Luke S. Snyder; Maureen C. Stone; Jeffrey Heer
abstract: To direct attention and communicate context, visualization designers often employ augmentations such as annotations, animated transitions, and stylistic layouts. While graphical perception principles can helpfully prescribe effective low-level representations of data, they lack guidance for augmentations that service higher-level communication goals. To bridge this gap, we contribute a design space that frames designer intent as viewer-oriented cognitive behaviors, grounding communicative aims in actionable visualization design techniques, including both visual encodings and augmentations. This design space consists of common augmentation tactics (annotation, animation, stylized encodings, etc.) that implement design strategies (spotlighting, sequencing, association, etc.) to achieve higher-level design goals (observe, interpret, introspect), often simultaneously. We demonstrate the analytic and generative value of our design space with examples across varied designer objectives. We discuss how our contributions help align designer intent with reader takeaways, pave the way for readers to learn more effectively, and enable future (semi-)automated systems to support visualization designers in achieving their communication goals.

title: XL MIMO Extreme Learning Machines: Wave-Domain Inference with Stacked Metasurfaces
authors: Kyriakos Stylianopoulos; Mattia Fabiani; Davide Dardari; George C. Alexandropoulos
abstract: The recently envisioned goal-oriented communications paradigm requires machine learning inference to be performed directly on wirelessly transferred data, by splitting neural network computations between the transmitter, the Receiver (RX), and the wireless channel. Such approaches aim to offload large portions of the computation onto the channel itself, which is often controlled by reconfigurable MetaSurfaces (MSs). Typical MS-parametrized systems, however, enable only limited computation offloading in the wave domain, usually corresponding to a single neural network layer, due to adverse channel fading effects and the almost linear operation of the channel and conventional MS models. In this paper, we demonstrate that an eXtremely Large (XL) Multiple-Input Multiple-Output (MIMO) system equipped with Stacked Intelligent MSs (SIM) at the RX side, together with a single antenna and its accompanying radio-frequency chain, may act as a two-layer neural network operating exclusively over the air. The first (uncontrollable) network layer corresponds to the transformations offered by wireless fading, while the second (controllable) layer is implemented via SIM operations. In particular, only the first, front-end MS layer needs to exhibit nonlinear response to serve as an activation function. Leveraging the Extreme Learning Machine (ELM) framework, the proposed XL MIMO system architecture is shown to be a universal approximator, and the optimal linear-SIM-based combining is derived in closed form, allowing for fast training even and partial signal observability. Numerical evaluations across diverse datasets showcase that the proposed XL-MIMO-ELM framework achieves classification accuracy comparable to idealized digital models, thereby, proving the viability of low complexity, wave-domain neural computations.

title: Goal-Oriented Bundle Management and Flow Control for Deep-Space Communications via Reinforcement Learning
authors: Sajjad Baghaee; Aimin Li; Shanmugarajan Balasubramanian; Elif Uysal
abstract: Deep-space communications operate under intermittent connectivity, long propagation delays, and relay storage constraints. In such networks, the Bundle Protocol enables store-carry-forward communication, requiring relay nodes to manage limited storage and scarce contact opportunities. Relay-side scheduling and dropping decisions are inherently goal-oriented: transmission resources should be allocated to bundles most valuable to downstream mission objectives. Conventional schedulers, such as FIFO, do not explicitly optimize task utility and may provide unfair service across heterogeneous planetary sources. This paper presents a closed-loop modeling and learning framework for relay-side bundle and flow management in a contact-driven deep-space network, where lunar and Martian updates are forwarded through a shared-buffer relay to Earth. We quantify destination-side information freshness using excess age $Δ_i^e(t)=[Δ_i(t)-d_i(t)]^+$, where $Δ_i(t)$ denotes the Age of Information of source $i$ and $d_i(t)$ is a source-dependent delay baseline. Based on this metric, we define a goal-oriented loss that supports source-dependent nonlinear penalties, allowing prioritization according to mission relevance. We formulate relay control as a constrained semi-Markov decision process (CSMDP) and solve it using masked Lagrangian Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). Feasibility-aware action masking restricts transmissions to bundles that can complete within the remaining contact window. DTNSim simulations indicate improved age-based utility and inter-flow fairness compared with baseline schedulers. The proposed framework jointly optimizes relay-side bundle scheduling, dropping, and flow control under contact-driven dynamics with explicit fairness considerations across heterogeneous sources.

title: Goal-Oriented Ordered Autoencoding for Successive Refinement in Progressive Communication
authors: Qi Liao; Dario Bega
abstract: Goal-oriented communication often struggles to sustain downstream task performance under variable and unpredictable bandwidth. We address this problem by proposing GO-OAE (Goal-Oriented Ordered AutoEncoding), which learns a progressively refinable quantized latent sequence, optimized directly for task utility rather than source reconstruction. Each component of the sequence is represented for transmission by its code index, and the learned ordering enables inference from any received prefix of the index sequence, with performance improving as more indices arrive. We prove that optimizing the goal-oriented distortion objective is equivalent to solving a weighted conditional information bottleneck formulation, and introduce an unbiased multi-prefix importance sampling (MPIS) estimator, to reduce GO-OAE training computational cost from O(BK) to O(Bm) with m << K, and reduces the estimator variance by a factor of 1/m. Experiments show that, on MiniImageNet, GO-OAE achieves over 96% of the lossless upper-bound classification accuracy using 324 bits per image (683X compression vs. raw RGB), and already attains over 94% of the upper bound with only 70% of the transmitted indices. It consistently outperforms reconstruction-optimized codecs and ordered autoencoders trained with uniform prefix sampling across all transmission budgets, demonstrating effective communication at extreme compression rates.

title: Behavior-Mining, Generative Conversations, and Collaborative Advisory: the Future of Travel and Tourism Recommender Systems
authors: Alejandro Bellogín; Linus W. Dietz; Francesco Ricci; Pablo Sánchez
abstract: Since the early adoption of e-commerce, travel and tourism has been a lab for the design of recommender systems: tools that help travelers choose destinations, flights, accommodations, and combine them into itineraries. Data-driven recommendation techniques, ranging from case-based reasoning to reinforcement learning, have been adapted to travelers' needs. The research community has produced multifaceted prototypes of travel and tourism recommender systems (TTRSs), which are context-dependent, multistakeholder-oriented, and more recently, addressing sustainability issues, such as overtourism. Despite this enduring work, TTRSs are not widespread yet. We argue that three limitations can explain this: outdated and sparse data sets used to train and validate TTRSs, algorithms that prioritize prediction accuracy over domain-specific dimensions such as novelty and contextual relevance, and a failure to address the specific needs of travelers. Targeted incremental research could address these limitations, but a disruptive factor has meanwhile entered the ecosystem of tourism information and commercialization platforms: generative artificial intelligence. According to market research, GenAI applications are becoming the primary entry point for travelers planning their trips. This forces research to rethink how TTRSs should be designed and which core techniques should be integrated. We claim that future TTRSs, in addition to offering personalized information filtering, should become more flexible advisors that support decision making, integrating multiple data types and AI techniques, from data mining to natural language processing. Moreover, they must transparently balance the conflicting goals of travelers, service suppliers, platform owners, and local communities. We then outline research targets for building more effective TTRSs, fruitfully combining old and new recommendation techniques.

title: Algorithmic Justice and Responsible AI Journalism: A Comparative Communication Policy Perspective in East Asia
authors: Renxiudi Huang; Linjia Bai
abstract: As generative artificial intelligence and automated content curation rapidly reshape the global media landscape, the intersection of algorithmic justice and media governance has become a critical frontier for sustainable development. This study provides a comparative communication policy analysis of China and South Korea, focusing explicitly on how their distinct regulatory toolkits address the tension between algorithmic fairness and platform accountability in AI journalism. While China utilizes a top-down, state-centric regulatory framework emphasizing ideological security, algorithmic registration, and strict synthetic media labeling, South Korea employs a multi-stakeholder co-regulation model driven by personal data protection, anti-monopoly platform intervention, and civil society oversight. Through a detailed textual analysis of key policy documents—including China's Provisions on the Administration of Algorithmic Recommendations and South Korea's Guidelines for AI Service Ethics to Protect Users—alongside empirical evidence from prominent algorithmic news curation platforms (Toutiao and Naver), this paper evaluates the implementation efficacy and structural trade-offs of each nation's approach. We demonstrate that while both models mitigate the risks of digital infodemics and algorithmic bias, they face contrasting trade-offs between regulatory efficiency and editorial independence. Finally, this study introduces the "Policy-Media-Society" (PMS) responsive governance framework, clarifying how systemic institutional adaptations can advance UN Sustainable Development Goal 16 (SDG 16) by ensuring public access to transparent, verified information.

title: Krum-Inspired Central Teacher Selection and Residual Channel Bottlenecks for Efficient DeepSC
authors: Rami Eid; Mostafa Jammoul; Omar Kaaki; Maria Slim; Mariette Awad; Hadi Sarieddeen
abstract: Deploying transformer-based semantic communication models on edge devices requires compression that preserves semantic fidelity under channel variability. We study a compressed deep semantic communication (DeepSC) student trained by multi-teacher knowledge distillation and combine two ideas: (i) a residual channel bottleneck that splits the transmitted representation into a base stream and a residual stream with unequal power allocation, and (ii) a Krum-inspired, medoid-style centrality criterion that selects a single central teacher from a five-model ensemble, applied at the logit and intermediate-feature levels and combined with a feature-dominant distillation loss. On the EuroParl benchmark, a two-layer student recovers about 98% of the four-layer teacher's bilingual evaluation understudy (BLEU)-1 under additive white Gaussian noise, with 93% of its BLEU-4 and 96% of its sentence-BERT (SBERT) score, and about 89%, 77%, and 87% of the teacher's BLEU-1, BLEU-4, and SBERT, respectively, under Rayleigh fading, while reducing non-embedding parameters by 1.33x and single-teacher inference latency by 1.79x (9.0x relative to a five-teacher ensemble used here as an upper-bound reference, not a deployment baseline). Controlled ablations over three seeds indicate complementary contributions of about +8.4% BLEU-1 (+9.6% SBERT) from the residual bottleneck and +3.0% (+2.9% SBERT) from centrality-based selection over mean aggregation. A decoder-mode ablation shows that the base stream alone recovers about two-thirds of the full BLEU-1 while the residual stream alone collapses, supporting the role of the residual as a refinement on top of the base.

title: Where to Defend? Layer-Wise Adversarial Training for Robust Transformer-Based Semantic Communications
authors: Maria Slim; Razane Tajeddine; Mariette Awad; Hadi Sarieddeen
abstract: Deep learning-based semantic communication (DeepSC), a Transformer-based encoder-decoder, achieves semantic fidelity over noisy channels but remains vulnerable to adversarial perturbations injected at multiple stages of the pipeline. We present a layer-wise robustness framework that compares fast gradient sign method (FGSM), projected gradient descent (PGD), and l2-normalized fast gradient method (FGM) defenses at the embedding output, and then uses PGD to analyze three attack and defense points: the embedding output, encoder output, and channel-encoder bottleneck. We evaluate reconstruction on Europarl and UK Hansard and sentiment classification on SST2 and YELP under additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) and Rayleigh fading. A first-order damage budget, {epsilon} times the l1 norm of the clean-input loss gradient at each injection point, predicts the attack-severity ordering, and the transfer matrix reveals asymmetric defense transfer: the embedding defense transfers strongly to encoder attacks, whereas encoder defenses degrade robustness against upstream attacks. For reconstruction, encoder-point training yields the largest matched gain but fails severely under embedding attacks; joint embedding-plus-encoder training retains comparable gains under encoder attacks while mitigating this mismatch failure, and Rayleigh fading attenuates robustness gains and degradation. For classification, three of four defenses collapse to constant predictors; only the channel-encoder defense remains non-degenerate, suggesting a protective role for the 128D-to-16D bottleneck. At a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 9 dB and perturbation budget {epsilon} = 0.3, the matched encoder defense recovers bilingual evaluation understudy (BLEU) from ~ 0.10 to ~ 0.64 on Europarl/AWGN, whereas the mismatched encoder defense yields a -0.444 BLEU change relative to the undefended baseline under an embedding attack.

title: Semantic-Aware Sub-Band Allocation for Terahertz Communications
authors: Fatima Ismail; Hadi Sarieddeen; Jihad Fahs
abstract: This paper studies semantic-aware sub-band al- location for terahertz (THz) communication systems, where frequency-selective molecular absorption creates highly non- uniform sub-band qualities. Unlike conventional formulations, semantic fidelity depends nonlinearly on the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and is also sentence-specific, leading to a non-separable assignment problem that is generally not solvable using simple ordering-based policies. To address this, we use a sentence-BERT (SBERT)-based surrogate model that predicts semantic fidelity from the sentence embedding and sub-band SNR. We propose an importance-aware scheduler that assigns sentences to sub- bands based on their semantic contribution using an oracle utility function that captures importance-weighted semantic similarity across sentence-sub-band pairs. A neural scheduler is then trained through imitation learning to approximate the oracle policy at more than 200x lower runtime than full DeepSC- based oracle evaluation. Integrated with a deep-learning-enabled semantic communication (DeepSC) system, the proposed method consistently outperforms all benchmark schemes and approaches oracle-level performance under realistic THz channel conditions.

title: Flexible Deep Joint Source-Channel Coding: A Vibrotactile Example
authors: Shuijie Li; Kemi Chen; Runjie Wang; Tiesong Zhao; Xiaoming Tao
abstract: The increasing demand for real-time tactile communication in multimedia systems has exposed the limitations of existing Joint Source-Channel Coding (JSCC) techniques. While current JSCC models facilitate end-to-end optimization, they typically operate at fixed coding rates and require separate model instances for different rate settings. This results in significant storage overhead and limited adaptability to dynamic bandwidth conditions. To address these challenges, we propose the Flexible Deep Joint Source-Channel Coding (FD-JSCC) framework for vibrotactile signals, which supports flexible-rate transmission without the need for model switching. The FD-JSCC integrates a flexible-rate encoder-decoder enhanced with Hierarchical Gain Adaptation Module (HGAM) and Rate-Switchable Residual Module (RSRM), enabling bitrate-aware compression by selectively preserving salient vibrotactile features. Additionally, we introduce a Channel Feature Processing Module (CFPM), which leverages real-time SNR information to enhance robustness against channel noise and signal degradation. Trained on the IEEE 1918.1.1 vibrotactile dataset, FD-JSCC achieves reconstruction performance comparable to fixed-rate baselines (e.g., DeepSC-S), while reducing storage requirements by 61.1\% when supporting four rates. These results underscore its potential for scalable, low-latency tactile communication in next-generation networks.

title: Compressibility is not Feedback: A Random-access Gap in Causal Semantic Repair
authors: Milad Bafarassat
abstract: Semantic feedback can repair a noisy first decode without retransmitting the whole message, but current end-to-end evaluations hide where a feedback design fails. An oracle that sees both the source-side state and receiver observation may describe a useful correction with few bits, while the receiver, which sees only its own observation, may not know which correction to request. We formulate these as distinct direct and receiver-constrained coding problems, connect repair distortion to retained local utility and prove a random-access separation: one direct bit is exact although receiver utility vanishes with the number of source-conditioned alternatives. A synthetic ladder verifies the exact law. In paired populations of eight Reuters text-JSCC codecs, the trained recurrent population retains over three times more direct 16-bit repair value than the trained DeepSC population despite comparable full-repair opportunity. Nevertheless, an entropy-valid receiver audit across all eight recurrent checkpoints does not resolve against repetition, source-only or shuffled-index controls. The results show that compressible repair is an upper bound, not evidence of deployable feedback, and motivate reporting both rate curves under matched resources.
